Hydrocarbons.intro: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that is separated by fractional distillation.
Hydrocarbons.mnemonic: Fractions from top to bottom go from Gas to Bitumen — 'Great Petrol Keeps Nice Diesel For Bitumen' (Gases, Petrol, Kerosene, Naphtha, Diesel, Fuel oil, Bitumen).

sections.title: Crude Oil
sections.text: Crude oil is a naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient marine organisms over millions of years.
points: Formation — ancient marine organisms buried under sediment; heat and pressure over millions of years
Non-renewable — takes millions of years to form; will eventually run out
Mixture of hydrocarbons — many different chain lengths from CH₄ to very long molecules
Fossil fuel — alongside coal and natural gas; burning releases CO₂ contributing to climate change
Finite resource — drives need for alternative fuels and sustainable energy sources
Extraction — drilled from underground reservoirs; transported by pipeline or tanker

sections.title: Fractional Distillation
sections.text: Crude oil is separated into fractions based on the different boiling points of its components using a fractionating column.
points: Heated and vaporised — crude oil is heated at the base; vapours rise up the column
Temperature gradient — column is hottest at the bottom, coolest at the top
Condensation at different levels — each fraction condenses when it reaches its boiling point level
Shorter chains at top — lower boiling point, more flammable, less viscous, more volatile
Longer chains at bottom — higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
Fractions (top to bottom) — gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen

sections.title: Properties and Uses of Fractions
sections.text: The physical properties of each fraction determine how it is used — shorter chains make better fuels; longer chains are used for lubricants and road surfaces.
points: Gases (LPG) — methane, propane; used for cooking and heating
Petrol — C5–C10; used as car fuel; low viscosity, highly flammable
Kerosene — C10–C16; jet fuel and heating oil
Diesel — C14–C20; heavy vehicle fuel; more viscous than petrol
Fuel oil — ships and power stations
Bitumen — C70+; road surfacing; very high boiling point; very viscous

keyTerms.def: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms
A naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient organisms over millions of years — a non-renewable fossil fuel
A physical separation process that separates a mixture based on differences in boiling points
A group of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and boiling points, collected at one level of the fractionating column
Resistance to flow — longer hydrocarbon chains are more viscous
Easily evaporated; short-chain hydrocarbons are more volatile due to lower boiling points

examTips: Shorter carbon chains = lower boiling point = more flammable = less viscous = more volatile. These properties are linked — learn them together.
Fractional distillation is a PHYSICAL separation — no chemical bonds are broken and no new substances are formed.
In the fractionating column, fractions condense at different levels — they do NOT boil off at the top.
commonMistakes: Confusing fractional distillation (physical separation, no new substances) with cracking (chemical decomposition into new molecules).
Saying lighter fractions (shorter chains) have higher boiling points — it is the opposite; shorter chains have lower boiling points.
Saying crude oil is a compound — it is a MIXTURE of many different hydrocarbon compounds.
clozePassages: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms. They are the main components of crude oil, which is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths. Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation — the mixture is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column and condense at different levels depending on their boiling points. Shorter chains have lower boiling points and are more flammable.

Crude oil is a finite, non-renewable resource formed over millions of years from the remains of marine organisms. It is extracted by drilling and refined by fractional distillation. The fractions obtained include petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, and bitumen. Each fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar chain lengths and boiling points. Crude oil is the raw material for many important products including fuels and plastics.

The physical properties of hydrocarbons depend on the length of their carbon chains. Shorter chains are more volatile (evaporate easily), have lower boiling points, and are less viscous. Longer chains have higher boiling points and are more viscous. These properties affect their uses — short-chain hydrocarbons are used as fuels (petrol, LPG) while long-chain hydrocarbons are used as lubricants and road surfacing (bitumen).

Alkanes.intro: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — they contain only single C-C bonds. They are the main components of crude oil fractions.
Alkanes.mnemonic: Methane, Ethane, Propane, Butane — 'Many Energetic Purple Butterflies' (M=1C, E=2C, P=3C, B=4C). Formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — add 2 to double the carbons!

sections.title: Alkane Structure
sections.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single C-C bonds, following the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
points: General formula — CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (e.g. n=1: CH₄; n=2: C₂H₆; n=4: C₄H₁₀)
Saturated — only single C-C and C-H bonds; no double bonds present
First four alkanes — methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀
Homologous series — each member differs by CH₂; gradual change in physical properties
Relatively unreactive — strong C-C and C-H bonds; do NOT decolourise bromine water
Isomers — same molecular formula, different structural arrangement; e.g. butane and methylpropane (both C₄H₁₀)

sections.title: Combustion of Alkanes
sections.text: Alkanes burn in oxygen. Complete combustion produces CO₂ and water; incomplete combustion produces toxic CO and soot.
points: Complete combustion (excess O₂) — hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O; clean blue flame
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂) — produces carbon monoxide (CO) and/or soot (carbon particles); yellow/orange smoky flame
Carbon monoxide hazard — colourless, odourless, toxic gas; binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport
Worked example — complete: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; incomplete: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O
Soot (carbon) — unburnt carbon particles; causes respiratory problems and blackens surfaces
Environmental impact — CO₂ from combustion is a greenhouse gas contributing to climate change

sections.title: Properties and Uses
sections.text: The properties of alkanes change predictably as chain length increases, making different alkanes suitable for different purposes.
points: Boiling point increases with chain length due to stronger intermolecular (van der Waals) forces
Methane (CH₄) — natural gas; used for heating and cooking
Propane and butane — LPG (liquefied petroleum gas); camping stoves, portable heaters
Petrol fraction — C5–C10 alkanes; car fuel
Substitution reactions — with halogens in UV light; e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (slow without UV)
Industrial importance — alkanes from crude oil power most of the world's transport and energy needs

keyTerms.def: A saturated hydrocarbon with only single C-C bonds; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
A hydrocarbon containing only single bonds between carbon atoms — no double bonds
Burning in excess oxygen producing only carbon dioxide and water
Burning in limited oxygen producing carbon monoxide (CO) and/or soot (carbon)
A family of compounds with the same general formula; each member differs by a CH₂ unit; similar chemical properties
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements; same atoms, different connectivity

examTips: Complete combustion = CO₂ + H₂O (clean, excess O₂). Incomplete combustion = CO + C (toxic soot, limited O₂). Always state which type in balanced equations.
Alkanes are saturated — they do NOT decolourise bromine water. Only alkenes (unsaturated) decolourise bromine water.
When balancing combustion equations, balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen last.
commonMistakes: Saying incomplete combustion produces CO₂ — it produces CO (carbon monoxide), not CO₂.
Confusing saturated alkanes (single bonds, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) with unsaturated alkenes (double bond, CₙH₂ₙ).
Forgetting that carbon monoxide (CO) is dangerous because it is colourless and odourless — it cannot be detected without a detector.
clozePassages: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. They have only single carbon-carbon bonds. The first four alkanes are methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈), and butane (C₄H₁₀). Alkanes are relatively unreactive because the C-C and C-H bonds are strong and non-polar. However, they undergo combustion reactions with oxygen and substitution reactions with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion of alkanes occurs with excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion occurs when oxygen is limited, producing carbon monoxide (a toxic gas) and soot (carbon particles). Complete combustion releases more energy than incomplete combustion. In car engines and gas boilers, ensuring complete combustion is important for both efficiency and safety.

Alkanes form a homologous series — a family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, where each member differs by a CH₂ unit. As chain length increases, boiling point increases due to stronger intermolecular forces. All alkanes burn in oxygen. Their structural formulae show the arrangement of atoms — isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures, giving them different physical properties.

Alkenes.intro: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a C=C double bond. They are more reactive than alkanes and used to make polymers.
Alkenes.mnemonic: Alkenes are UNSATURATED — think of them as 'hungry' for more atoms! The double bond is like an open hand ready to grab atoms in addition reactions. 'Double bond = double the reactivity!'

sections.title: Alkene Structure
sections.text: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons characterised by at least one C=C double bond, following the general formula CₙH₂ₙ.
points: General formula — CₙH₂ₙ (e.g. n=2: C₂H₄ ethene; n=3: C₃H₆ propene)
C=C double bond — makes alkenes UNSATURATED; source of their reactivity
First three alkenes — ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, butene C₄H₈
More reactive than alkanes — the C=C double bond readily undergoes addition reactions
Bromine water test — alkenes decolourise orange bromine water to colourless; alkanes do not
Used to make polymers — ethene → poly(ethene); propene → poly(propene)

sections.title: Test for Alkenes
sections.text: Bromine water is the standard test to distinguish between alkenes (unsaturated) and alkanes (saturated).
points: Bromine water (orange/brown) — add to unknown hydrocarbon and shake
Alkene present → decolourises to colourless (bromine adds across the C=C double bond)
Alkane present → stays orange (no reaction at room temperature without UV light)
Reaction with Br₂ — ethene + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane; addition reaction
UV light and alkanes — alkanes only react with bromine in UV light (substitution, not addition)
Significance — distinguishes saturated from unsaturated compounds; important after cracking

callout.label: Bromine Water Test
callout.text: Add bromine water (orange). Alkene present → decolourises to colourless. Alkane → no change (stays orange).

sections.title: Addition Reactions
sections.text: Alkenes undergo addition reactions where the C=C double bond opens and atoms add across it to form a single product.
points: Principle — the C=C double bond opens; atoms add across it; single bond replaces double bond
Hydrogenation — alkene + H₂ → alkane; nickel catalyst, 150°C; e.g. ethene + H₂ → ethane
Hydration — alkene + H₂O (steam) → alcohol; phosphoric acid catalyst; e.g. ethene + H₂O → ethanol
Halogenation — alkene + Br₂ → dibromoalkane; this is what decolourises bromine water
100% atom economy — all reactant atoms end up in the single product; no waste
Addition polymerisation — repeated addition of alkene monomers; ethene → poly(ethene)

keyTerms.def: An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one C=C double bond; general formula CₙH₂ₙ
A hydrocarbon containing at least one C=C double bond — has room to accept more atoms
A reaction where atoms add across a C=C double bond to form a single product
Addition of H₂ across a C=C double bond, converting an alkene to an alkane; requires nickel catalyst
Addition of water (steam) across a C=C double bond to form an alcohol; requires acid catalyst
The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product; addition reactions have 100% atom economy

examTips: Bromine water test: alkenes decolourise it (orange → colourless); alkanes do NOT. This is the key test for unsaturation.
Addition reactions produce only ONE product — that is why they have 100% atom economy. State this in evaluation questions.
In hydration of ethene: ethene + steam → ethanol. This is how ethanol is made industrially from crude oil (not fermentation).
commonMistakes: Saying alkanes decolourise bromine water — only ALKENES do this because they have the C=C double bond for addition reactions.
Forgetting that addition reactions produce only ONE product — students sometimes list two products.
Confusing hydration (alkene + water → alcohol) with fermentation — hydration uses ethene from cracking, not glucose.
clozePassages: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one carbon-carbon double bond. The general formula is CₙH₂ₙ. The simplest alkene is ethene (C₂H₄). The double bond makes alkenes more reactive than alkanes. They readily undergo addition reactions, where the double bond opens up and atoms are added across it. Alkenes decolourise bromine water — this is a test for unsaturation.

Alkenes undergo addition reactions. With hydrogen (hydrogenation), the double bond is broken and a single bond forms — ethene becomes ethane. With water (hydration), ethanol is produced — this is how ethanol is manufactured industrially. With halogens such as bromine, dihalogenoalkanes are produced. The bromine water test distinguishes alkenes from alkanes — alkenes decolourise bromine water while alkanes do not.

Addition polymerisation uses alkene monomers to form polymers. Ethene monomers join together under high pressure and temperature with a catalyst to form poly(ethene). Propene forms poly(propene). The double bonds in the monomers open up and form single bonds between monomers in the polymer chain. These polymers have many uses — packaging, fibres, and plastics. The repeat unit of the polymer has the same atoms as the monomer but with a single bond.

Cracking.intro: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones. It is essential because demand for shorter-chain fractions exceeds supply.
Cracking.mnemonic: Cracking = Breaking BIG into small. Think of CRACKING an egg: you break something large (shell) to get what's useful inside. Always makes at least one ALKENE — the C=C double bond is the crack!

sections.title: Why Crack?
sections.text: Crude oil contains more long-chain fractions than are needed, and not enough short-chain fractions. Cracking addresses this imbalance.
points: Supply and demand imbalance — too many long-chain fractions (fuel oil, bitumen); not enough petrol and diesel
Converts surplus to useful products — breaks long chains into shorter, more valuable ones
Produces alkenes — essential feedstocks for manufacturing polymers (plastics)
Thermal decomposition — cracking is a chemical change, not a physical one like distillation
Economic importance — increases value of crude oil by converting low-value fractions to high-value ones
Feeds polymer industry — ethene from cracking is the starting material for poly(ethene) production

sections.title: Types of Cracking
sections.text: Two main methods are used industrially: thermal cracking at high temperature and catalytic cracking using an aluminium oxide catalyst.
points: Thermal cracking — 700°C or higher; high pressure (up to 70 atm); no catalyst needed; mainly produces alkenes
Catalytic cracking — lower temperature (~500°C); aluminium oxide (zeolite) catalyst; mainly produces branched alkanes and aromatic compounds for petrol
Both are thermal decomposition — C-C bonds are broken using heat energy
Vapour passed over catalyst — in catalytic cracking, the long-chain vapour is passed over hot catalyst
Products depend on method — thermal → more alkenes; catalytic → more petrol-grade alkanes
Steam cracking — another term for thermal cracking using steam; used in industrial polymer feedstock production

sections.title: Products of Cracking
sections.text: Cracking always produces at least one alkene alongside shorter alkane chains, which can be confirmed with bromine water.
points: Always produces at least one alkene — the C=C double bond distinguishes cracked products from fractions
Worked example — decane (C₁₀H₂₂) → octane (C₈H₁₈) + ethene (C₂H₄); check: 10C=8+2; 22H=18+4+2×2
Smaller alkane produced — can be used as fuel (petrol range) or further processed
Testing with bromine water — cracked products decolourise bromine water; confirms alkene present
Multiple products possible — same starting molecule can crack in different ways
Mass is conserved — total number of C and H atoms on each side of the equation must balance

callout.label: Example
callout.text: Decane (C₁₀H₂₂) → octane (C₈H₁₈) + ethene (C₂H₄). Always produces at least one alkene.

keyTerms.def: A thermal decomposition reaction that breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones
Cracking using an aluminium oxide (zeolite) catalyst at around 500°C; produces branched alkanes and alkenes
Cracking at high temperature (700°C+) and high pressure without a catalyst; mainly produces alkenes
Unsaturated product of cracking containing a C=C double bond; used to make polymers
A reaction where a compound is broken down into simpler substances using heat
A raw material used as the starting point for making other chemicals; alkenes from cracking are polymer feedstocks

examTips: Cracking always produces at least one alkene — this is essential for polymer production and is frequently tested.
Cracking is thermal decomposition (a chemical change) — do not confuse with fractional distillation which is a physical separation.
When balancing cracking equations, check carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms balance on both sides. The products must include at least one alkene.
commonMistakes: Saying cracking only produces alkanes — it always produces at least one alkene (otherwise it's not cracking).
Confusing cracking (chemical change, new substances) with fractional distillation (physical separation, no new substances).
Forgetting to balance cracking equations — count C and H atoms on both sides to verify.
clozePassages: Cracking is the process of breaking long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones. It is carried out by heating the hydrocarbon to a high temperature and passing the vapour over a hot catalyst (catalytic cracking) or by heating to a very high temperature with steam (steam cracking). Cracking produces alkanes and alkenes, which are used as fuels and as raw materials for making polymers.

Crude oil contains more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed and less short-chain hydrocarbons. Cracking converts the unwanted long-chain fractions into more useful shorter molecules. This includes petrol and other fuels, and alkenes such as ethene for making polymers. The cracking reaction produces a mixture of products. Alkenes are identified by their ability to decolourise bromine water.

There are two main types of cracking. Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at moderate temperatures and produces branched alkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons, useful as petrol. Steam cracking uses high temperatures and steam and produces more alkenes, which are feedstocks for polymer production. Both types reduce the supply of long-chain fractions and increase the supply of more economically valuable shorter-chain products.

Polymers.intro: Polymers are very long chain molecules formed by joining many small monomer units together. Plastics are synthetic polymers.
Polymers.mnemonic: POLYMER = Poly (many) + Mer (units). Think 'Many MERmaids in a long chain holding hands — each one is a monomer, together they're a POLYMER!' Needs C=C to start the chain.

sections.title: Addition Polymerisation
sections.text: Addition polymerisation joins unsaturated alkene monomers together, opening the C=C double bond to form a long chain polymer with no other products.
points: Requires C=C double bond — only unsaturated (alkene) monomers can undergo addition polymerisation
Double bond opens — forms single bonds between monomers in the chain
Only ONE product — the polymer; no other molecules produced = 100% atom economy
Conditions — high temperature and pressure, with a catalyst
Ethene → poly(ethene) — used in plastic bags, bottles, packaging
Propene → poly(propene) — used in ropes, carpets, containers

sections.title: Naming Polymers
sections.text: Polymers are named by placing 'poly' in front of the monomer name in brackets. The repeat unit structure shows single bonds in place of the double bond.
points: Naming rule — poly(monomer name); e.g. ethene → poly(ethene); propene → poly(propene)
Repeat unit — shows one monomer unit in the chain with a bond extending each side
Drawing polymers — show the repeat unit in brackets with n outside; single bond replaces double bond
PVC — poly(chloroethene); monomer is chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl); used in pipes, window frames
PTFE — poly(tetrafluoroethene); non-stick coating on pans
Polystyrene — poly(phenylethene); packaging, insulation

callout.label: Naming Rule
callout.text: Put 'poly' in front of the monomer name in brackets. E.g. ethene → poly(ethene). Propene → poly(propene).

sections.title: Issues with Plastics
sections.text: Synthetic polymers create significant environmental problems because they are not biodegradable and persist in ecosystems for hundreds of years.
points: Non-biodegradable — most synthetic polymers cannot be broken down by microorganisms; persist for centuries
Microplastics — tiny plastic fragments enter food chains; found in oceans, soil, and human tissue
Landfill — much plastic ends up in landfill; takes up space and can leach chemicals
Recycling — different polymers must be sorted before recycling; reduces waste but not all plastics are recyclable
Combustion for energy — burning plastic releases energy but produces CO₂ and toxic gases
Biodegradable alternatives — polymers made from plant starch; break down naturally but currently expensive

keyTerms.def: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined together in a long chain
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer
A reaction where alkene monomers join through their C=C double bonds to form a polymer — no other products
The structural unit that repeats throughout the polymer chain — shown in brackets with n subscript
Capable of being broken down by microorganisms — most synthetic polymers are NOT biodegradable
The proportion of reactants converted into desired product; addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy

examTips: Monomers for addition polymerisation MUST have C=C double bonds — alkenes only, not alkanes.
Name polymers correctly: poly(ethene) not polyethene — the brackets are required in the AQA notation.
Addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy — only ONE product (the polymer) is formed.
commonMistakes: Using alkanes as monomers for addition polymerisation — they have no double bond; you need alkenes.
Forgetting the brackets in polymer names — AQA expects poly(ethene) with brackets around the monomer name.
Drawing the repeat unit with a double bond — it should have a single bond; the double bond opens up during polymerisation.
clozePassages: Addition polymers are formed from alkene monomers. The C=C double bond opens and monomers join in long chains. Poly(ethene) is used in plastic bags and bottles. Poly(propene) is used in ropes and containers. PVC (poly(chloroethene)) is used in pipes and window frames. The properties of the polymer depend on the monomer — chain length, branching, and cross-linking all affect strength and flexibility.

Condensation polymers form when monomers with two functional groups react, releasing a small molecule such as water. Polyester is made from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid. Nylon is a polyamide made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. Unlike addition polymers, condensation polymers have functional groups within the main chain. They can often be broken down by hydrolysis, which reverses the condensation reaction.

Disposing of polymers is a major environmental challenge. Most synthetic plastics are not biodegradable and persist in the environment for hundreds of years. Options include recycling, which requires sorting different polymer types. Some plastics can be broken down by combustion to recover energy. Biodegradable polymers made from plant starch are being developed as a more sustainable alternative. Reducing plastic use and improving recycling infrastructure are key priorities.

Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids.intro: Alcohols and carboxylic acids are important functional group families. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are the key examples.
Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids.mnemonic: Alcohols have -OH (think: OH! That's a drink). Carboxylic acids have -COOH (CO Oh! That's acidic). Ester = Alcohol + Carboxylic Acid → a fruity ESTER (think ESTER the fruit fairy).

sections.title: Alcohols
sections.text: Alcohols are a homologous series characterised by the hydroxyl (-OH) functional group, with ethanol being the most important example.
points: Functional group — -OH (hydroxyl group); this determines alcohol chemistry
General formula — CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
First three — methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propanol C₃H₇OH
Uses — ethanol as fuel (biofuel), solvent (perfumes, medicines), in alcoholic drinks
Fermentation — glucose + yeast → ethanol + CO₂; anaerobic; 30°C; C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
Hydration of ethene — C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH; steam + phosphoric acid catalyst; continuous industrial process

sections.title: Carboxylic Acids
sections.text: Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH functional group and are weak acids. They react with alcohols to form esters.
points: Functional group — -COOH (carboxyl group); makes these compounds weakly acidic
Weak acid — only partially ionise in water; lower pH than strong acids at same concentration
Ethanoic acid CH₃COOH — the main example; found in vinegar; makes pH 3-4 in solution
React with metals — produce hydrogen gas (like other acids)
React with carbonates — produce CO₂, water and a salt
Esterification — alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water (acid catalyst, e.g. H₂SO₄)

sections.title: Esters
sections.text: Esters are formed by the reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid. They have characteristic fruity smells and are used in flavourings and perfumes.
points: Formation — alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water (reversible; acid catalyst)
Naming esters — first part from alcohol (e.g. ethyl from ethanol); second from acid (e.g. ethanoate from ethanoic acid)
Example — ethanol + ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate + water
Fruity smells — used in perfumes, food flavourings (e.g. banana, pear, pineapple)
Uses — solvents (nail varnish remover), flavourings, plasticisers
Hydrolysis — esters can be broken back down into alcohol + acid using water and acid/base catalyst

keyTerms.def: An organic compound containing the -OH (hydroxyl) functional group; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
An organic compound containing the -COOH (carboxyl) functional group; a weak acid
A compound formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid in an esterification reaction; has fruity smell
Anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast enzymes at 30°C to produce ethanol and CO₂
The reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water; requires acid catalyst
An acid that only partially ionises in water, releasing fewer H⁺ ions than a strong acid at the same concentration

examTips: Fermentation equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Remember: anaerobic (no oxygen), yeast, 30°C, slow.
Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water (with acid catalyst). The ester name = alcohol part + acid part.
Ethanoic acid is a WEAK acid — it does not fully ionise. Do NOT confuse with strong acids like HCl or H₂SO₄.
commonMistakes: Confusing the -OH functional group (alcohols) with the -COOH functional group (carboxylic acids) — learn both and which is which.
Saying fermentation uses oxygen or needs aerobic conditions — fermentation is specifically ANAEROBIC (no oxygen).
Thinking ethanoic acid is a strong acid — it is a WEAK acid and only partially ionises in water.
clozePassages: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (-OH). The simplest alcohol is methanol (CH₃OH), followed by ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and propanol (C₃H₇OH). Ethanol is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks, produced by fermentation of sugars. Alcohols are used as fuels, solvents, and in perfumes. They react with sodium to produce hydrogen gas and are oxidised to form carboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl functional group (-COOH). The simplest is methanoic acid, followed by ethanoic acid (found in vinegar). They are weak acids, partially ionising in water. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters and water — this is esterification. Esters have fruity smells and are used in perfumes and food flavourings.

Ethanol can be produced in two ways. Fermentation uses yeast to convert glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide — this is a slow process carried out at 30°C, suitable for making alcoholic drinks. Hydration of ethene with steam and an acid catalyst is a fast, continuous industrial process. Fermentation uses renewable plant material; hydration uses ethene from crude oil. Both methods have advantages depending on the context.
